claim: The efficient coding principle accounts for the allocation of computational resources in central sensory processing when sampling an image is the main limitation.
source: Using the visual system as a model, we recently showed that the efficient coding principle accounted for the allocation of computational resources in central sensory processing: when sampling an image is the main limitation, resources are devoted to compute the statistical features that are the most variable, and therefore the most informative (eLife 2014;3:e03722. DOI: 10.7554/eLife.03722 Hermundstad et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous publication (Hermundstad et al., 2014) that demonstrated this relationship.

claim: Resources are devoted to compute the statistical features that are the most variable, and therefore the most informative, when sampling an image is the main limitation.
source: when sampling an image is the main limitation, resources are devoted to compute the statistical features that are the most variable, and therefore the most informative (eLife 2014;3:e03722. DOI: 10.7554/eLife.03722 Hermundstad et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Hermundstad et al., 2014).

claim: Computations involving sensitivity to specific multipoint correlations take place in visual area V2, primarily in its supragranular layers.
source: Building on these results, we use single-unit recordings in the macaque monkey to determine where these computations—sensitivity to specific multipoint correlations—occur. We find that these computations take place in visual area V2, primarily in its supragranular layers.
evidence: The claim is based on single-unit recordings presented in this manuscript.

claim: V2 neurons are sensitive to the multipoint correlations that are informative about natural images.
source: The demonstration that V2 neurons are sensitive to the multipoint correlations that are informative about natural images provides a common computational underpinning for diverse but well-recognized aspects of neural processing in V2, including its sensitivity to corners, junctions, illusory contours, figure/ground, and 'naturalness.'
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: V2 sensitivity to multipoint correlations provides a common computational underpinning for V2's sensitivity to corners, junctions, illusory contours, figure/ground, and 'naturalness.'
source: The demonstration that V2 neurons are sensitive to the multipoint correlations that are informative about natural images provides a common computational underpinning for diverse but well-recognized aspects of neural processing in V2, including its sensitivity to corners, junctions, illusory contours, figure/ground, and 'naturalness.'
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings and established knowledge about V2 properties.

claim: The statistics that were the most variable were the most salient perceptually.
source: Specifically, we analyzed the local statistics of natural images, and compared the variability of these statistics with their perceptual salience. The statistics that were the most variable—that is, the least predictable and therefore the most informative—were the most salient perceptually.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Hermundstad et al., 2014).

claim: The relationship in which greater resources are allocated to more variable features emerges from the efficient coding principle in the regime that the main constraint is input sampling.
source: This relationship, in which greater resources are allocated to more variable features, emerges from the efficient coding principle in the regime that the main constraint is input sampling (Barlow, 1961; van Hateren, 1992; Doi and Lewicki, 2014; Hermundstad et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to theoretical work.

claim: The observed relationship contrasts with the 'whitening' regime, which emerges when the main constraint is output capacity.
source: The observed relationship contrasts with the more familiar 'whitening' regime (Srinivasan et al., 1982), which emerges when the main constraint is output capacity (e.g., with regard to the retina and the optic nerve bottleneck); the whitening regime predicts that fewer resources are allocated to more variable features.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Srinivasan et al., 1982) and established knowledge about efficient coding regimes.

claim: The whitening regime predicts that fewer resources are allocated to more variable features.
source: the whitening regime predicts that fewer resources are allocated to more variable features.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the whitening regime in efficient coding theory.

claim: Input sampling, rather than output capacity, is the main constraint in central visual processing.
source: We note that the results of (Hermundstad et al., 2014) provide empirical support for the hypothesis that input sampling, rather than output capacity, is the main constraint—since a transmission limit would have predicted a lower sensitivity for image statistics that were the most variable, the opposite of what we found.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the results of Hermundstad et al., 2014.

claim: Analyzing natural images via multipoint correlations reduces the dimensionality of the space of image statistics that need to be considered.
source: To reach this result, we analyzed natural images via their multipoint correlations, that is, the statistics of the combinations of luminance values that appear in several points of the image. This approach has several advantages. First, it reduces the dimensionality of the space of image statistics that need to be considered, since it can be applied to binarized images, and it separates informative from uninformative statistics (Tkačik et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tkačik et al., 2010.

claim: The multipoint correlation approach separates informative from uninformative statistics.
source: it reduces the dimensionality of the space of image statistics that need to be considered, since it can be applied to binarized images, and it separates informative from uninformative statistics (Tkačik et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tkačik et al., 2010.

claim: The multipoint correlation approach enables rigorous tests of theoretical predictions by isolating individual kinds of informative and uninformative multipoint correlations in synthetic image sets.
source: Second, the approach enables rigorous tests of theoretical predictions, since the individual kinds of informative and uninformative multipoint correlations can be isolated in synthetic image sets (Victor and Conte, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Victor and Conte, 2012.

claim: Multipoint correlations in natural images covary in a complex manner that is difficult to capture or control.
source: In contrast, the multipoint correlations in natural images covary in a complex manner that is difficult to capture or control.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the complexity of natural image statistics.

claim: Synthetic image sets that isolate individual kinds of multipoint correlations are highly un-natural.
source: Synthetic image sets that isolate individual kinds of multipoint correlations are highly un-natural, but here this is an advantage: our predictions, which are derived from natural images, are tested in an out-of-sample fashion.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the construction of the synthetic stimuli.

evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Victor and Conte, 1989.

claim: V2 sensitivity to multipoint correlations does not require a close match between RF size and the scale of the multipoint correlation.
source: Figure 2—figure supplement 1 (right column) shows that V2 sensitivity to multipoint correlations also does not require a close match between RF size and the scale of the multipoint correlation; this sensitivity is present over a threefold range of length scales (i.e., a 10-fold range of the number of checks per receptive field).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: V2 sensitivity to multipoint correlations is present over a threefold range of length scales (a 10-fold range of the number of checks per receptive field).
source: this sensitivity is present over a threefold range of length scales (i.e., a 10-fold range of the number of checks per receptive field).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The entire range of scales relevant to perception can be accounted for by the properties of individual neurons, along with the variation in RF sizes at each eccentricity.
source: Thus, it is likely that the entire range of scales relevant to perception can be accounted for by the properties of individual neurons, along with the variation in RF sizes at each eccentricity (Hubel and Wiesel, 1968).
evidence: This is an inference from the data, combined with knowledge about RF size variation cited from Hubel and Wiesel, 1968.

claim: Neurons whose RFs are difficult to map are often ignored in physiologic studies.
source: Neurons whose RFs are difficult to map are often ignored in physiologic studies (Olshausen and Field, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Olshausen and Field, 2004.

claim: Many V2 neurons whose RFs could not be mapped nevertheless often showed selective sensitivity to multipoint correlations.
source: We were able to analyze their responses here because of the tetrode recording method, and found that many V2 neurons whose RFs could not be mapped nevertheless often showed selective sensitivity to multipoint correlations.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data.

claim: Standard practice is to use random binary stimuli for RF mapping procedures.
source: Standard practice is to use random binary stimuli for this mapping procedure (Reid et al., 1997)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Reid et al., 1997.

claim: Inclusion of stimuli with high-order correlations in the mapping computation allows some kinds of nonlinear responses to emerge in a first-order cross-correlation between stimulus and response.
source: The rationale is that inclusion of these stimuli allows some kinds of nonlinear responses to emerge in a first-order cross-correlation between stimulus and response, because of correlations within the stimuli (Schmid et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Schmid et al., 2011.

claim: Reverse correlations may not exceed statistical threshold because of response variability, or because the neuron is only responsive to stimulus configurations that occur very rarely in the stimulus set.
source: Reverse correlations may not exceed our statistical threshold because of response variability, or because the neuron is only responsive to stimulus configurations that occur very rarely in the stimulus set.
evidence: This is speculation about reasons why some neurons do not have mappable RFs.

claim: For each of the ensembles that probe a different kind of multipoint correlation, the number of black and white checks are equated, at each location.
source: We also note that from a computational point of view, our assay for sensitivity to multipoint correlations is independent of whether the neural response is correlated with the state of any single check: for each of the ensembles that probe a different kind of multipoint correlation, the number of black and white checks are equated, at each location.
evidence: This is a property of the stimulus construction method.

claim: It is possible for a neuron to process information in a localized region of space yet fail to have a RF that is measurable by reverse correlation methods.
source: Thus, it is quite possible for a neuron to process information in a localized region of space (as manifest by its sensitivity to multipoint correlations) yet fail to have a RF that is measurable by reverse correlation methods, as we show here.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Many biologically-plausible mechanisms can extract multipoint correlations, including a simple linear-nonlinear cascade and modulatory surrounds.
source: Many biologically-plausible mechanisms can extract multipoint correlations, including a simple linear-nonlinear cascade (provided that the nonlinearity is more than quadratic), and modulatory surrounds (Schmid and Victor, 2014; Self et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schmid and Victor, 2014 and Self et al., 2014.

claim: The specificity of responses to multipoint correlations can be produced by a two-stage (linear-nonlinear-linear-nonlinear) cascade, in which the first linear-nonlinear element detects local edges, and the second one combines signals from collinear edges via a second threshold.
source: In this regard, we note (Victor and Conte, 1991) that the specificity we observe can be produced by a two-stage (linear-nonlinear-linear-nonlinear) cascade, in which the first linear-nonlinear element detects local edges, and the second one combines signals from collinear edges via a second threshold.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Victor and Conte, 1991.

claim: Removal of either the linear or the nonlinear element of the second stage eliminates the specificity of responses to multipoint correlations.
source: Removal of either component of the second stage—either its linear or the nonlinear element—eliminates this specificity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Victor and Conte, 1991.

claim: Responses to multipoint correlations being more prominent in supragranular V2 than in its input layers or in V1 suggests possible correspondences between the two-stage cascade and neural circuitry.
source: The finding that responses to multipoint correlations are more prominent in supragranular V2 than in its input layers or in V1 suggests possible correspondences between this cascade and neural circuitry.
evidence: This is speculation about the neural implementation of the computational model.

claim: One possibility is that the first stage of the two-stage cascade is in V1 and the second stage is in V2.
source: One possibility is that the first stage is in V1 and the second stage is in V2 (Wilson et al., 1992; Rust et al., 2005).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Wilson et al., 1992 and Rust et al., 2005.

claim: Alternatively, the two linear-nonlinear stages may represent two loops of signal passage through a recurrent network within a single cortical area.
source: Alternatively, the two linear-nonlinear stages may represent two loops of signal passage through a recurrent network within a single cortical area (Joukes et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Joukes et al., 2014.

claim: Check size was scaled to the RF size of the target neuron so that approximately two checks corresponded to one lobe of the optimal spatial frequency.
source: Check size was scaled to the RF size of the target neuron so that approximately two checks corresponded to one lobe of the optimal spatial frequency, and orientation was set according to the orientation preference of the target neuron.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: About 8 checks were within the classical RF (V1: mean 7.40, median 6.00, SD 5.33; V2: mean 8.68, median 7.00, SD 5.46).
source: This resulted in about 8 checks within the classical RF (V1: mean 7.40, median 6.00, SD 5.33; V2: mean 8.68, median 7.00, SD 5.46; statistics across all mappable units and not just the target; see below for details on RF mapping and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for the distribution of number of checks in the RF)
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data.

claim: The checks are within the resolution limits of the neuron, and the stimulus patch covers an area that is substantially larger than the RF.
source: thus, the checks are within the resolution limits of the neuron, and the stimulus patch covers an area that is substantially larger than the RF.
evidence: This is an inference from the stimulus design.

claim: Across all recordings, check sizes ranged from 0.08 to 0.5 deg (V1: mean 0.18, median 0.20, SD 0.05; V2: mean 0.22, median 0.20, SD 0.12).
source: Across all recordings (including mappable and un-mappable units), check sizes ranged from 0.08 to 0.5 deg (V1: mean 0.18, median 0.20, SD 0.05; V2: mean 0.22, median 0.20, SD 0.12).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data.

claim: For each type of stimulus, 1024 examples (two repetitions each) were presented for 320 ms, interleaved in a pseudorandom sequence.
source: For each type of stimulus, we presented 1024 examples (two repetitions each) for 320 ms, interleaved in a pseudorandom sequence.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The large set size was chosen to distinguish average responses to each of the stimulus sets from responses that might be driven to the specific white or black checks or edges present in particular examples.
source: This large set size was chosen so that we can distinguish average responses to each of the stimulus sets (our focus) from responses that might be driven to the specific white or black checks or edges present in particular examples (a potential confound).
evidence: This is an explanation of the experimental design rationale.

claim: Stimuli were generated via a Markov recurrence rule so that other than the constraint of their defining multipoint correlation, they are as random as possible (maximum-entropy).
source: Stimuli were generated via a Markov recurrence rule (Victor and Conte, 1991, 2012), so that other than the constraint of their defining multipoint correlation, they are as random as possible (maximum-entropy).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Victor and Conte, 1991, 2012.

claim: In each stimulus set, there are no two-point correlations—checks at any pair of locations are colored independently.
source: In each set, there are no two-point correlations—checks at any pair of locations are colored independently—so that the sets have the same power spectra, and therefore the same spatial frequency content.
evidence: This is a property of the stimulus construction method.

claim: The stimulus sets have the same power spectra, and therefore the same spatial frequency content.
source: so that the sets have the same power spectra, and therefore the same spatial frequency content.
evidence: This is a property of the stimulus construction method.

claim: The four kinds of correlations (the even/odd axis, the black triangle/white triangle axis, wye, and foot) are independently controlled: each set extremizes one of these correlations, while keeping all the others at 0.
source: The four kinds of correlations (the even/odd axis, the black triangle/white triangle axis, wye, and foot) are independently controlled: each set extremizes one of these correlations, while keeping all the others at 0 (Gilbert, 1980).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gilbert, 1980.
